docs.title: Review given: Ghani's pilah-mobile #162, 23 Oct
docs.text:
Ghani's PR removes the Ekspor action (PDF and Excel) from the draft pencairan editor. It changes one line of the header and removes the _export handler, three imports and the export widget tests. It adds eight tests asserting that no export action exists on a new, saved, confirmed or cancelled draft, at phone and desktop width. The description calls it the first stage of a removal.

Review

Verified before commenting, on the PR head 38dc9cf:

  • The suite passes: flutter test test/features/draft_pencairan gives 413 passing tests.
  • Mutation check: I restored staging's editor page, with the Ekspor button, and ran the new draft export is unavailable group. 8 of 8 failed. The new tests really guard the removal; they don't pass by default.
  • No unrelated coverage lost: only export tests were removed from draft_editor_view_test.dart.
  • No remaining entry point: I searched the PR head, and nothing in the app reaches the export path any more.
  • No decision on record: Linear has no issue for removing it. The feature was delivered under PIL-316, which is Done.
Point Why it matters Suggestion 1. Which decision removes this? (question) A feature delivered and closed in PIL-316 disappears with no linked decision. QA or the sprint review could read it as a regression. Link the standup or PO decision, or open a Linear issue for the removal. 2. Track the follow-up cleanup After the PR, ExportMenuButton, DraftPdfPreviewPage, simpanBerkasDraft/bagikanBerkasDraft, DraftEditorCubit.export with EditorPhase.exporting and canExport, the repository's exportDraft, and the backend's draft_export.py are unreachable, but still compiled, tested and counted by Sonar. canExport still reads as if export were possible. A Linear issue with that list, each item linked to its line on the PR head, so the second stage isn't forgotten. 3. Show the RED in history The description walks through RED, GREEN and REFACTOR, but it is one feat commit, so only the mutation check above shows that the tests went red first. Separate [RED], [GREEN] and [REFACTOR] commits, as on the other pencairan PRs.

I posted this as a comment rather than an approval: the code is right, but (1) is a product decision that should be on record first. None of the points blocks the change itself.

docs.title: AI Literacy
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

AI used critically:

  • Its claims were checked against the code, a clean staging checkout or a control build before anything changed.
  • Its own wrong turns were caught and reported, not smoothed over: a wrong test expectation, a skill step that dirtied tracked files, a redaction pass that broke a script, a scan report that came out empty.
  • One claim it made was shown incomplete by human reviewers: the race fix on #137. It's recorded that way, along with the fix that followed, proven by a test that really races.

Decisions with team or outside impact were put to me: where to point a pen test, whether to create a Linear issue, and how to post a review.

Evidence for this week:

  • Session export: Claude Code's own /export of the session behind 26–29 Oct, with home-folder paths shortened to ~. It was taken at 22:36 on 29 Oct, so it ends before the #137 review fixes. Those are recorded in their commits and review replies.
  • The PRs, review and reports linked below, each of which records the checks described here.

docs.title: How AI was used this week
docs.text:
• Tool: Claude Code as an agent in VS Code, across pilah-be, pilah-mobile and pilah-docs. Linear through Composio; GitHub through gh; SonarCloud's API; Playwright with Edge against local builds; OWASP ZAP through its API.
  • Guardrails:
    • the workspace skills (ship's layout, tdd), and the code-review skill for #178;
    • CI's own commands, run locally before every push;
    • rules kept in memory, applied without being restated:
      • the TDD phase in every commit subject;

  • My role:

docs.title: Where verification changed the outcome
docs.text: Situation What happened 26 Oct: QA suggested a back button that resets the chosen role on the phone Before agreeing, it traced the role to the server: saved the moment Lanjutkan is tapped, and pinned by a backend test. It said a phone-only reset couldn't work and rated the finding High rather than Critical, with reasons. It created the Linear issue only after I said yes. 26 Oct: Its first test expected 400 for a forbidden role The mutation check showed the API's handler answers 422 {"errors": …}. It fixed the test to the project's convention, not the code, and said the assumption was its own. 26 Oct: The ship skill's ".agents copy" step In these repos .agents is tracked, so copying the outdated canonical copy dirtied two tracked files in the new worktree. It spotted that in git status, restored them, and later wrote a worktree script that skips the copy when .agents is tracked. 26 Oct: 5 backend and 25 mobile tests failed locally It didn't call them pre-existing until it had run them on a clean staging checkout, where they fail the same way, because of Windows paths. 26 Oct: The design lints can't run on Windows Instead of skipping them, it counted their patterns by hand against the baselines and caught its own breach: a hard-coded font size over the allowed count. Fixed before CI. 26 Oct: SonarCloud showed 97.1% where local said 100% It found that a PR's CI runs only the changed test files, and that two pre-existing methods counted as new lines. It added the two tests rather than explaining the number away. 26 Oct: "The conditional UPDATE closes the race" This claim was incomplete. Tristan and Pascal showed that a registration already past its role check can still link a bank afterwards. The AI's own race test had pre-linked the bank, so it never exercised that order. On 29 Oct it accepted the finding without arguing, wrote a test that really races (two threads on PostgreSQL) and watched it fail on all three paths, including accept_invite, which the review hadn't named. Then it fixed all three with a shared row lock and answered each thread. 29 Oct: Making the race test fully covered The fix left one line of the test that only runs while the bug exists. It reworked the test, then re-ran it against the pre-fix code to prove it still fails there, instead of assuming the change was harmless. 26 Oct: Pen test target An active scan sends thousands of attack requests. It asked whether to scan local or staging and listed the trade-offs. I chose local only. 26 Oct: ZAP reported 17 Medium It triaged each one against the production nginx.conf and the real servers, separating local artifacts from real findings. It reproduced the 500 with curl, and found the same crash in terbitkan, which ZAP had missed. 26 Oct: Its own tooling misled it twice The ZAP report came out empty (a wrong site separator in its call), and the E2E script showed 4 "failures" (Django 6 prints a banner before the output). It noticed both were its own mistakes, fixed them, and reran. Neither became a reported bug. 29 Oct: A redaction pass for the Linux handover Its automatic secret filter rewrote a harmless local test login in a copied script, which would have broken it. A byte-for-byte comparison against the originals caught it, and the filter was narrowed to CLI output only. 29 Oct: Reviewing #178 It expected the CDN script to be blocked, but the browser reported eval. It traced the real cause into the dependency's source, proved the regression against a control build, and, in the review, didn't claim an untested alternative (pdfrx) would work.

docs.title: A critical complexity finding on my own code
docs.text:
Rule Severity Where Opened Closed dart:S3776 Cognitive Complexity Critical CompleteProfileScreen.build: "reduce its Cognitive Complexity from 17 to the 15 allowed" 26 Oct, 20:48 WIB 26 Oct, 22:00 WIB, fixed

The role note had added an Authenticated check and a three-part condition to a build method that was already near the limit. docs.title: A design-lint breach, caught by hand
docs.text:
The team's test/design/* tests limit hard-coded colours and font sizes per file, against *_baseline.json. On Windows, 19 of them always fail: the baseline is keyed with / paths and Windows yields \, so every file reads "allowed 0". They fail the same way on a clean staging checkout, so a local run can't tell me anything.

So I checked them by hand. I grepped every line this MR adds for the lints' patterns, and counted per file against the baselines.

  • My new role note's TextStyle(fontSize: 13, …) raised complete_profile_screen.dart from its allowed 1 hard-coded font size to 2, which would have failed CI.
  • 00fec19 switched it to AppTextStyle.small, which brought the count back to 1.
  • A final scan found no other lint pattern in the added lines. CI agreed: "Format, analyze, tests & build" passed.

docs.title: Local checks before every push
docs.text:
These are the commands CI runs, run locally first.

Backend (#137), against Postgres 16:

$ ruff check . && ruff format --check .                        # all checks passed
$ pip check                                                    # no broken requirements
$ python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run             # no changes
$ python manage.py check --deploy --fail-level ERROR           # passes (warnings only)
$ mypy api apps config shared_kernel tests                     # no issues in 221 files
$ coverage run … manage.py test && diff-cover … --compare-branch=origin/staging
                                                               # 878 tests; 100% of the changed lines

mypy caught a missing api.models.__all__ export before the push, fixed in 8bf93cf. The 5 failing backend tests are deployment-script tests that need bash paths and LF line endings. They fail the same way on a clean staging checkout on Windows, and pass in CI.

Mobile (#174):

$ dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed lib test codegen   # 0 changed
$ flutter analyze                                                    # no issues
$ flutter test --coverage                                            # the same 25 Windows-only failures as staging, nothing new
$ diff-cover coverage/lcov.info --compare-branch=origin/staging      # 100% of 70 changed lines
$ flutter build web --release -t lib/main_development.dart           # built

The debug APK couldn't be built locally: Android's google-services.json isn't on this machine, and CI supplies it from a secret. PIL-451 changes no Android or native code, and CI's build passed.

docs.title: Development Discipline
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

Two meaningful merge requests this week, the backend and mobile halves of one QA finding:

  • pilah-be #137: PATCH /onboarding/role, 13 commits;
  • pilah-mobile #174: "Ganti peran" and the role page, 14 commits.

Both come from one Linear issue I wrote from the QA note, and both use the same branch (feature/pil-451) off staging. Every commit is a scoped Conventional Commit:

  • the TDD phase is in each subject;
  • the OWASP category is in the subject where it applies;
  • the body names the design issue, the pattern and its origin.

Each MR description has the cause, the API contract, the red/green table, the E2E results with screenshots, and the local validation. Tool findings and review findings were fixed as new commits, never force-pushed, and each review thread got a reply linking its fix. Neither MR is merged yet; they wait for approval (see below).

docs.title: From QA note to two MRs
docs.text:
1. Checked before it was called a bug. QA suggested resetting the chosen role on the phone. Tracing it showed the role is saved on the server the moment Lanjutkan is tapped, and nothing could change it afterwards. A test pins that on purpose. So a phone-only reset couldn't work, and the fix needed both repos.
  2. Rated, not assumed: High, not Critical. Nothing is lost or exposed, but a mis-tap is a permanent dead end on the first screen, and testers on fresh Google accounts would hit it before UAT on 6 Nov.
  3. Tracked in Linear. I created PIL-451 as a sub-issue of CPBI-34 in Cycle 3. It has the cause, the severity, backend and mobile tasks, and the tests to write, in the same layout as my earlier PIL-374.
  4. One branch name in both repos: feature/pil-451, so Linear links both PRs to the issue.
  5. Test-first, in slices: three red/green pairs plus two mutation-proven guards on the backend, four pairs and two refactors on mobile. The tables are on the TDD page.
  6. CI's own checks run locally before each push:
    • backend: ruff, pip check, makemigrations --check, migrate, check / check --deploy and mypy, then the suite on Postgres 16;
    • mobile: flutter analyze, dart format, the full suite, diff coverage, and the web build.

docs.title: Example commit messages
docs.text:
feat(onboarding): [GREEN] refuse a role change once onboarding has started (PIL-451, OWASP A04, A01)

change_role is now one conditional UPDATE: it only touches the row
while the profile is incomplete, there is no bank sampah (pending
included) and no linked membership. Otherwise 409 role_locked, and the
role stays.

Design issue: check-then-act. Reading the state, then saving, leaves a
window where a bank registration commits in between and is left under a
role it no longer matches.
Pattern: guarded state transition, done as a conditional UPDATE, so the
database re-checks the row as it writes it (the same technique as
_reactivate_rejected_membership). Origin: designed in.

The UPDATE does not run User.clean, so the membership condition is part
of the filter itself. The refusal is a clean 409, not the 500 that
clean's ValidationError gave (OWASP A01), and the onboarding state
machine is enforced on the server, not trusted to the client (OWASP A04).

test(onboarding): [RED] add failing test for changing role from Lengkapi Profil (PIL-451)

QA suggested a way back from Lengkapi Profil to the role choice. The
profile step must:

- name the role being registered ("Mendaftar sebagai Pengurus Bank
  Sampah") with a "Ganti peran" link that opens the role page on top,
  so back returns to the form;
- hide the link once a bank sampah exists for the account, and when
  joining through an invite (the backend refuses those anyway);
- redraw for the new role once the session switches to it: a nasabah
  gets "Pilih Bank Sampah" as step two, not "Data Bank Sampah".

Fails: there is no label or link. And with the label assertion
removed, the redraw check still fails, because the screen only listens
to the auth state and keeps drawing the old role's stepper.

The full subject lists read as a sequence of phases. Mobile, oldest first:

feat(onboarding): [GREEN] change role through PATCH onboarding/role and keep its session (PIL-451)
test(preview): cover the preview session's changeRole (PIL-451)
test(onboarding): [RED] add failing test for switching the session to a changed role (PIL-451)
feat(onboarding): [GREEN] switch the session to a changed role, or say why not (PIL-451)
test(onboarding): [RED] add failing test for picking another role from the role page (PIL-451)
feat(onboarding): [GREEN] let a signed-in account pick another role on the role page (PIL-451)
test(onboarding): [RED] add failing test for changing role from Lengkapi Profil (PIL-451)
feat(onboarding): [GREEN] name the role on Lengkapi Profil with a way to change it (PIL-451)
refactor(onboarding): [REFACTOR] name the role page's two Lanjutkan paths in _submit (PIL-451)

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

Standard principles applied and shown in PIL-451's two MRs:

  • All five SOLID principles, each with the code it applies to. See SOLID in this week's code.
  • Concurrency handled explicitly. A conditional UPDATE came first; when review showed it was half the race, a row lock shared by every writer of the invariant replaced it, reached across contexts through a port.
  • An append-only audit log for a privilege change.
  • Session renewal when the privilege level changes.
  • One page serving two entry states, decided once.
  • A single source of truth for role titles.
  • Extract Method, once from a SonarCloud finding and once on my own initiative.

Each item names the design issue it addresses, the pattern or principle used, its type and where the issue came from.

docs.title: Design issues and the patterns that address them
docs.text: Code Design issue Pattern / principle Type Origin change_role Check-then-act across two writers: the role change and each registration check the account, then write later, so either can slip in between First a guarded state transition (one conditional UPDATE), then a pessimistic row lock shared by every writer: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the account row before deciding Technique (concurrency) The UPDATE was designed in. It was incomplete: my own defect, found in review (Tristan's P1). Fixed with the lock in df45397 lock_for_onboarding A cross-context concern: bank_sampah must take a lock that authentication owns, without reaching into its services A port (hexagonal / ports and adapters): the authentication context exposes the lock through apps.authentication.api Architectural Designed in, following the project's existing ports UserRoleChangeLog (from role) A double tap could log a transition that never happened First a compare-and-set on the role read; since the lock, a second change waits and reads the role the first left Technique (serialization) Designed in, simplified by the lock UserRoleChangeLog No accountability for a privilege change Audit Log (Fowler): an append-only row per change, written in the same transaction, same shape as BankSampahApprovalLog Architectural Designed in (OWASP A09) _session_response A stale privilege in the token: the access token carries a role claim Renew the session on a privilege change (OWASP Session Management) Principle (security) Designed in (OWASP A07) The role page A create-only screen: the role page could only create an account, so a role saved on the server had no way back from the client One page, two entry states, decided once in initState; submit and listener branch on it, with no second page duplicating the cards Technique QA finding (PIL-451) on PIL-180's design titleFor Duplicated knowledge: Lengkapi Profil needs the role's display title, which the role page's options already define Single source of truth (DRY): a static query over the same _roleOptions the cards are drawn from Principle Designed in ref.watch A stale screen: after a role change, go_router returns to the same /complete-profile State, which still drew the old role's form Observer: the screen subscribes to the auth state and rebuilds when it changes GoF Behavioural (via Riverpod) Found by the red test in 9e83120 _changeableRoleTitle A long method mixing layout with a business rule: build at cognitive complexity 17 of 15 Extract Method (Fowler): a query method that names the rule Refactoring Tool finding on my own code (SonarCloud S3776) _submit A nested ternary choosing between two actions inside onPressed Extract Method Refactoring My own [REFACTOR]

docs.title: A guarded transition, then a shared lock — 52f087f, df45397
docs.text:
A role may change only while onboarding has committed nothing for it.

First version (52f087f): the conditions were part of one conditional UPDATE … WHERE, so the database re-checked the row as it wrote. It also replaced a 500: User.clean used to be the only thing stopping a linked member from changing role, and its ValidationError escaped unhandled.

The defect review found. Tristan (P1), with Pascal confirming the other side, showed it was only half the race:

  • register_bank_sampah checks user.role, then saves user.bank_sampah later;
  • register_nasabah and accept_invite have the same gap;
  • a role change committing in between still slipped through, because the UPDATE only saw links that were already committed.

The fix (df45397): every writer of this invariant takes the same row lock before deciding.

apps/authentication/services.py
@staticmethod
def lock_account(user: User) -> None:
    """Lock the account row for the caller's transaction and reload it.

    A role change and every onboarding write that checks the role
    (PIL-451) lock this same row, so they run one after the other: a bank
    or a membership is never linked under a role that changed after its
    check, and a role change sees whatever a finished registration
    linked. Call inside ``transaction.atomic()``.
    """
    User.objects.select_for_update().only("pk").get(pk=user.pk)
    user.refresh_from_db()
apps/authentication/services.py (change_role)
with transaction.atomic():
    OnboardingService.lock_account(user)
    if user.is_profile_complete or user.bank_sampah_id or user.keanggotaan_nasabah.exists():
        raise AuthServiceError(
            "Peran tidak dapat diganti setelah pendaftaran berjalan.",
            code="role_locked",
            status_code=409,
        )
    previous = user.role
    if previous != role:
        User.objects.filter(pk=user.pk).update(role=role, updated_at=timezone.now())
        UserRoleChangeLog.objects.create(user=user, from_role=previous, to_role=role)
apps/bank_sampah/services.py
@staticmethod
@transaction.atomic
def accept_invite(user: User, token: str) -> tuple[BankSampah, str]:
    lock_for_onboarding(user)
    # … the role check and the link to the inviting bank now see the locked row

bank_sampah reaches the lock through the authentication context's port, apps.authentication.api.lock_for_onboarding, not its services. The architecture test, which allows only apps.<bc>.api across contexts, still passes.

docs.title: The log cannot lie — 2c591c5
docs.text:
The audit row follows the project's existing approval logs: append-only, written only by the service, in the same transaction as the change. Because of the row lock, a second change waits for the first and reads the role it left. So a logged from_role is always the role the account really had.

apps/authentication/models.py
class UserRoleChangeLog(models.Model):
    """A role an account switched away from during onboarding (PIL-451).

    Written only by AuthService.change_role, in the same transaction as the
    change; rows are never edited.
    """

    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="role_change_logs")
    from_role = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=User.Role.choices)
    to_role = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=User.Role.choices)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

docs.title: A new session for a new privilege — 13c1a44
docs.text:
The endpoint answers with the same session payload as a Google login, built by the existing AuthService._session_response. So the new access token names the new role, and the client routes on next_step exactly as it does after registering.

Pascal noted that the old tokens aren't revoked: the access token lasts 24 h and the refresh token 30 d. Nothing reads a role from the token today, so it's harmless, but my PR description overstated it. I corrected the description to "the new tokens carry the new role" and stated the limit.

docs.title: One page, two entry states — 9517dbd
docs.text:
The role page served only a fresh Google registration, holding a registration token. Rather than copying its role cards into a second page, it decides once which kind of visit this is:

lib/features/authentication/presentation/pages/role_selection_page.dart
@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  final state = ref.read(authenticationProvider);
  _registration = _registrationFrom(state);
  if (_registration == null &&
      state is Authenticated &&
      state.authEntity.nextStep == 'complete_profile') {
    _account = state.authEntity;
    _selectedRole = GoogleRegistrationRole.values
        .where((role) => role.wireValue == state.authEntity.role)
        .firstOrNull;
  }
}

A success returns as a new Authenticated session, which the page's existing listener already routes through locationForAuthStep. A refusal comes back as a message, so the notifier never replaces the signed-in state with a failure state.

docs.title: Role titles from one place — a1b49bd
docs.text:
lib/features/authentication/presentation/pages/role_selection_page.dart
static String? titleFor(String? role) => _roleOptions
    .where((option) => option.value.wireValue == role)
    .firstOrNull
    ?.title;

docs.title: The screen follows the session — a1b49bd
docs.text: Lengkapi Profil used to only listen to the auth state, to catch a logout. After a role change, go_router returns to the same /complete-profile page with its State intact. So the screen now also watches the auth state, and redraws the new role's stepper and fields. The red test proved this before the change, with the label assertion removed.

docs.title: A rule out of a build method — 87f2f0d
docs.text:
SonarCloud flagged build (S3776, complexity 17 of 15) after the role note added an Authenticated check and a three-part condition. The rule now has a name:

lib/features/onboarding/presentation/pages/complete_profile_screen.dart
/// The title of the role this account registers as, while it may still be
/// changed (PIL-451): the role was saved on the role page and stays
/// changeable until a bank sampah is registered for it. An invite fixes the
/// role, so it gets none. Null when the note should not show.
String? _changeableRoleTitle(AuthenticationStates state) {
  if (_isInviteMode || state is! Authenticated) return null;
  if (state.authEntity.bankSampahStatus != null) return null;
  return RoleSelectionPage.titleFor(state.authEntity.role);
}

build now only places the note when it gets a title. In the same spirit, 2589b0b moved the role page's register-or-change choice out of onPressed into _submit.

docs.title: SOLID in this week's code
GoF design patterns in this week's code
docs.text:
Category Pattern Where + commit What it does Behavioural Observer (via Riverpod) ref.watch(authenticationProvider) in Lengkapi Profil, a1b49bd (mine). It joins the role page's ref.listen, which Tristan's Riverpod migration introduced (efd6748, #160, 24 Oct) One state change, a new session, reaches every subscribed screen. The role page routes on it, and Lengkapi Profil redraws for it.

The other structures this work builds on aren't GoF, so they're labelled as what they are:

  • Repository (Architectural, PoEAA): AuthRepository dates from the 2024 template (d2c9eb3). This week extends it.
  • Use case / Interactor (Architectural, Clean Architecture): LoginWithGoogleUseCase dates from June (910bad8). This week extends it.
  • Audit Log (Architectural): new this week in 2c591c5, shaped like the initial backend's approval logs.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Competency level: 1

This week's code guards and names four OWASP Top 10 categories in its commits: A01, A04, A07 and A09, each with tests. Level 2 needs at least five named in one week's commits, so this week claims level 1. I didn't stretch a fifth label to fill the gap.

This week's security work also includes a new dynamic scan with OWASP ZAP 2.17.0, explained, with a test-first patch plan: ZAP scan report, 26 Oct. It ran signed in, against my own local backend and web build, with every documented endpoint imported from the OpenAPI schema. It is recorded below, but not claimed as a level.

docs.title: The ZAP scan
docs.text:
0 High. Four real findings, each with a planned fix (full detail in the report):

# Finding OWASP Severity Planned fix 1 tarik and terbitkan crash (500) on a missing or malformed id. I reproduced it by hand; ZAP only caught tarik A04 Low–Medium Load through the bank-scoped get_object() (404), test-first 2 The backend CSP allows any HTTPS origin (script-src 'self' https: and three more directives) A05 Medium default-src 'none' for JSON; exact origins for the docs page and the OAuth popup 3 Swagger UI loads @latest from jsDelivr with no SRI A08 Low (debug-only) Pin it and add hashes, or serve it locally 4 The web app shell has no script-src A05 Low–Medium In progress as Pascal's #178; my review found one regression in it

Explained, not just listed. Of 15 alert types, the missing clickjacking and nosniff headers and the version-leaking Server header are local artifacts. Production nginx already sends those headers, and production doesn't run the dev servers. The report says why for each one, so the patch plan holds only real work.

docs.title: OWASP guards in this week's code
docs.text: OWASP category Guard Tests Commits A01 Broken Access Control Only registering roles may change a role; superadmin can be neither left nor reached; a linked member can't leave the bank's scope Anonymous 401, superadmin 403, asking for superadmin 422, linked member 409 (once an unhandled 500) e227286, 52f087f, cafba5a. The superadmin guards are mutation-proven A04 Insecure Design The onboarding state machine is enforced on the server; role changes and registrations serialize on the account row A completed profile, a pending bank or a linked membership gets 409; a two-thread race test on PostgreSQL for the bank, membership and invite paths e227286, 52f087f, bf3a529, f4b663d, df45397 A07 Identification and Authentication Failures A role change answers with a new session, so new tokens carry the new role The token's role claim is checked after the switch a23ba21, 13c1a44 A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures Every role change is written to user_role_change_log (account, from, to, when) in the same transaction One row per real change, none for a refusal or a re-pick 62e79e1, 2c591c5

docs.title: What review changed
docs.text:
• The A04 guard was incomplete, and is now fixed. Tristan's P1 showed that a registration whose role check ran before the role change could still link a bank afterwards. The fix (df45397) makes every writer lock the account row; accept_invite turned out to have the same gap and got the same fix (details).
  • The A07 guard is about new tokens only. The old access token (24 h) and refresh token (30 d) still carry the old role. Pascal noted it's harmless today, because nothing reads a role from the token. My PR description had overclaimed it, and now states the limit. Blacklisting the old refresh token is offered as a follow-up.

docs.title: Test Driven Development
docs.text:
Competency level: 4

Level 3 met: both PIL-451 MRs were built test-first, one behaviour per [RED] → [GREEN] pair, with the phase in every commit subject and [REFACTOR] commits only after green. Every changed line is covered: 100% on SonarCloud for both MRs, 48 and 68 new lines. The tests cover the positive case, the negative cases (each refusal) and the corner cases (a stale account object, re-picking the same role, a malformed response).

Level 4: advanced testing methods in the commits:

  • Mocks and fakes for isolation:
    • the mobile data layer runs the real AuthRepositoryImpl on mocktail mocks of its remote and local data sources;
    • captureAny captures the stored tokens to prove the new session is the one saved.
    • The notifier tests run the real AuthenticationNotifier on a mocked LoginWithGoogleUseCase. Page tests use a fake notifier that records changeRole and answers with a configured refusal or session.
  • A real race, made deterministic: a TransactionTestCase on PostgreSQL runs each registration in one thread, pausing right after its role check, and a role change in another. It's been checked both ways: all three paths fail without the row lock, and pass with it.
  • Guards proven by mutation: two tests passed when written. For each, I broke the code it guards, watched it fail, and reverted.
  • E2E with database assertions: Playwright drives the web build through Flutter's semantics tree at desktop and phone sizes, then checks the backend's database for the stored role and the audit row.

docs.title: Backend: pilah-be #137
docs.text:
Behaviour Red Green The red failed on An unfinished account switches role, and the new access token names the new role a23ba21 13c1a44 404: no route yet The role stays (409 role_locked) once the profile is complete, a bank sampah exists (pending included), or a membership is linked e227286 52f087f Two cases switched with 200. The linked member hit User.clean's ValidationError, an unhandled 500 Each change is recorded in user_role_change_log; a refusal or a re-pick of the same role writes nothing 62e79e1 2c591c5 'User' object has no attribute 'role_change_logs' Review P1: a role change during a bank registration, a membership application or an invite acceptance waits for it, then refuses (role_locked) f4b663d df45397 All three paths: {'changed': True, 'waited_for_registration': False}. The role flipped under a registration, which then linked a bank to a nasabah, or hit an unhandled ValidationError (membership)

Refactor after green: fe17440 makes the race test record its outcome on both paths. The "change went through" branch could only run while the bug existed, so diff-cover showed the test at 98.6%. I re-ran the reworked test against the pre-fix services, and all three cases still fail there.

Guard tests, proven by mutation. Both passed when written, so there was no red phase. I mutated the code, watched each test fail, then reverted. The mutations are recorded in the commit bodies:

  • cafba5a, who may change a role: anonymous gets 401, superadmin 403, and asking to become superadmin 422.
    • With IsAuthenticated in place of IsRegistrationRole, the test failed with 200: the superadmin had switched itself to nasabah.
    • With every role allowed in the serializer, it failed with 200: a nasabah had become superadmin.
  • bf3a529, the race. The account is loaded, then a bank sampah is registered, then the role change runs on the stale object. A check-then-save version failed with "AuthServiceError not raised": the pengelola was switched to nasabah.
apps/authentication/test_role_change.py
def test_a_bank_registered_after_the_account_was_loaded_still_keeps_the_role(self) -> None:
    user = self._fresh(User.Role.PENGELOLA)
    # Loaded by this request before a parallel one registered a bank sampah.
    stale = User.objects.get(pk=user.pk)
    bank = BankSampah.objects.create(
        nama="Bank Baru",
        alamat="Depok",
        no_hp_pic="+628111111111",
        status=BankSampah.Status.PENDING,
    )
    User.objects.filter(pk=user.pk).update(bank_sampah=bank)

    with self.assertRaises(AuthServiceError) as refused:
        AuthService.change_role(stale, User.Role.NASABAH)

    self.assertEqual(refused.exception.code, "role_locked")
    user.refresh_from_db()
    self.assertEqual(user.role, User.Role.PENGELOLA)

A wrong assumption in my own test, corrected. I first wrote that asking for superadmin returns 400. This API's exception handler answers validation errors with 422 {"errors": …}, so I fixed the test to the project's convention. The code was right.

What review added. Tristan showed that this test proves only one side of the race. It pre-links the bank, so a registration whose role check ran before the role change was never exercised. The P1 race test above does exercise it, with real threads and row locks:

tests/regression/identity/test_role_change_race.py
with patch.object(owner, method, paused):
    a = threading.Thread(target=registration, name="registration")
    a.start()
    self.assertTrue(reached.wait(WAIT), "registration never reached its write")
    b = threading.Thread(target=role_change, name="role-change")
    b.start()
    b.join(1.0)
    outcome["waited_for_registration"] = b.is_alive()
    proceed.set()
    a.join(WAIT)
    b.join(WAIT)

Thread A's registration pauses inside its write, after the role check. Thread B's role change must still be blocked a second later, which is only possible if both take the same row lock. Then A finishes, and B must come back with role_locked.

His P2 asked for success tests for every Google role, not just nasabah. d83b0c1 switches to each registration role from a different one. It passed as written, so I proved it with a mutation: with pengelola_induk removed from the serializer, its case failed with 422.

docs.title: Team Development Management
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

A detailed review of Pascal's pilah-mobile #178 (29 Oct), which adds HSTS and a real Content-Security-Policy to the web image. It answers the check his description asked for, a signed-in click-through, which he couldn't do himself:

  • verified signed in under the PR's exact headers, against a control build without them: 8 pages clean;
  • one regression found (the draft PDF preview on web) and traced to its cause in a dependency;
  • three feasible fixes for it, cheapest first, and one hardening suggestion with the concrete change.

The other side of reviewing is here too: Tristan's and Pascal's reviews of my #137. Each finding was checked against the code, fixed test-first, and answered in its own thread with the fix linked.

docs.title: Review given: Pascal's pilah-mobile #178, 29 Oct
docs.text:
The PR replaces the web image's frame-ancestors-only CSP with a full policy:

  • strict script-src, with no inline scripts or eval;
  • 'wasm-unsafe-eval' for CanvasKit;
  • Google Sign-In allowed;
  • 30 days of HSTS.

Its description says only the login page was tested, and asks someone to sign in and click through the app.

Review

Verified before commenting, on the PR head 4480886:

  • Same headers as production: I built the PR for web and served it with the exact add_header lines parsed from its nginx.conf. The only change was a local connect-src entry standing in for *.fly.dev.
  • Signed in: as the seeded demo Pengurus.
  • Recorded: each violation, through the browser's own securitypolicyviolation event.
  • Control: the same build, served without the CSP.
  • Read the config: no location block sets its own add_header, so nginx's inheritance quirk doesn't drop the headers on any path.
  • CI really runs the tests: the Docker-based header tests run in CI (ci.yml, line 71).
Page Violations with the PR's CSP Login and sign-in, Beranda, Nasabah, Jadwal, Harga, Laporan, Draft Pencairan list, Profil 0 Draft editor → Ekspor → PDF 1, script-src blocked eval. The preview never renders With the PR's CSP Same build, no CSP

Traced to its cause, not guessed. I expected the CDN script to be the problem, but the browser reported eval. The PDF library's (printing 5.14.3) web code runs window.eval('typeof pdfjsLib …') before it loads anything (printing_web.dart L57-L63). After that it would also load pdf.js from unpkg. So allowing unpkg wouldn't help, and adding 'unsafe-eval' would break the PR's own test.

Point Why it matters Suggestion 1. The draft PDF preview breaks on web Pengurus can reach it on web today, and it would spin forever after this deploys The CSP is right, so change the app instead. Cheapest first: (a) merge Ghani's #162, which removes draft export, before #178; (b) on web, skip the preview and download directly; (c) render with pdfrx, already a dependency, whose WASM loads from the same origin (not yet tested under the CSP). Add a browser check, so the next CSP change can't break it silently 2. connect-src https://*.fly.dev https://*.run.app It trusts every app on two shared hosting domains, and anyone can deploy one, so an XSS could send data out The image is the official nginx:1.28-alpine, which fills in /etc/nginx/templates/*.template with envsubst at startup, substituting only variables that are actually set, so $uri is safe. Move the config there with ${PILAH_API_ORIGIN}, set per environment

I posted it as a comment, not a change request. Point 1 goes away if #162 merges first, so the ask is to agree on the merge order. Point 2 was marked as a follow-up.

docs.title: AI Literacy
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

AI used critically: its claims checked against the code, GitHub and logs before being acted on, its direction corrected where it drifted from team decisions, and the prompt history published with personal data removed.

docs.title: How AI was used
docs.text:
• Tool: Claude Code as an agent in VS Code, across pilah-be, pilah-mobile, pilah-docs and Linear (through Composio): reading code, running tests and CI-equivalent checks, committing, opening PRs, replying to reviews.
  • Guardrails: the workspace skills (tdd, ship, ask-for-review), CI on Postgres, and standing rules I gave it this week and asked it to remember: phase-tagged TDD commits, replying inside each review thread, never merging branches (the lead does), and 3P updates in Bahasa.

docs.title: 24–28 Sep — where verification changed the outcome
docs.text: Situation What verification found The AI told me my pencairan PRs were not merged, because my commit SHAs were not on staging I asked "are you sure?". Rechecked through the PRs themselves: all six were merged that morning, squashed by the lead into one commit per repository, so my SHAs could never appear. Confirmed by content too: the staging API answers 401, not 404, on the new routes. The AI saved the rule "check PR state, not SHA ancestry" The AI's reading of the PO's "7-day" rule combined two limits (an edit window and a backdating limit) I corrected it: follow the PO's answers only. The Linear decisions were rewritten to her wording before any code was written Recording a PR comment promising to merge #19 into my stacked #32 I stopped it: merges belong to the lead. The comment was edited and the rule saved A Discord agreement to adopt a teammate's IsActiveNasabah class Checked against the code instead of taking the chat at face value: staging already had an equivalent IsNasabahRole, and JWT authentication already rejects inactive users, so the extra is_active check added nothing. The agreement was out of date before anyone acted on it Four review findings from the lead on #19 Each was reproduced before being fixed: the red tests showed history at Rp 7.001 against a stored Rp 7.000,50, a backdated payout accepted with 201, and a nasabah refused with 403 A local test failed after merging staging Diagnosed as my local .env enabling debug mode, and proved by rerunning with .env moved aside, instead of "fixing" a correct test #19's diff coverage read 97% Every uncovered line was traced with git blame to code merged in from staging by other members; the four fixes themselves are fully covered, and the page says exactly that rather than claiming 97% or 100% A production database dump pasted into the chat for migration testing The AI flagged that it held real names, emails, phone numbers and unexpired refresh tokens; it is kept out of every repository, and it is removed entirely from the published prompt history below Test counts drafted for the IR pages The AI caught its own error before publishing: the mobile baseline was 278, not 270, so PIL-230 added 16 tests, not 24 The emulator "just closed" Diagnosed from the emulator's verbose log (12 GB needed, 2.9 GB free on C:) instead of reinstalling; the invisible window was found at y = −947 and moved on screen A chat export offered as AI-literacy evidence Checked before use: it held only a startup banner from another session, so the history was built from this session's own transcript instead

docs.title: Example: challenging "your PRs are not merged yet"
docs.text:
When I asked whether I could test my features with the release APK, the AI answered confidently that my pencairan PRs were not on staging: its check looked for my own commit SHAs there and found none.

That contradicted what I knew from the team (the lead had said he was merging my stack), so I asked it directly: "Are you sure my pencairan feats not merged yet?"

Rechecking through the PRs themselves instead of through git ancestry showed:

  • All six PRs (backend #19, #32, #52 and mobile #26, #27, #33) had been merged that morning. The lead squash-merged each stack into one commit (da13b32, 41ccced), which is exactly why my original SHAs could never appear on staging.
  • The code was live: the staging API answered 401 (login required) on /api/v1/pencairan and /pencairan/:id/riwayat, where an unmerged route would answer 404.
  • The latest staging APK already contained the features, so I could test that day instead of waiting.

The AI acknowledged the mistake plainly ("I was wrong") and recorded the lesson as a standing rule: check merge state through the PR, then confirm by content, never by commit ancestry alone.

docs.title: Example: deciding instead of accepting the first design
docs.text:
PIL-230 first said only "edit pencairan". The AI's first analysis laid out three options (edit only non-money fields, correct through reversal entries as the SDS's append-only rule suggests, or edit in place) and pointed out the conflict with the SDS. I did not pick from that list on my own: I took the open questions to the PO and lead, the lead and PO disagreed on whether nasabah see old versions, and I chose the PO's version with the lead's approval. The AI then turned the decisions into a design and asked me where the answers still left room:

  • Should a backdated new payout be validated at its date, or rejected before the nasabah's last activity? I chose rejecting, which keeps every receipt exact.
  • May a pengurus edit a pencairan of a nasabah who is no longer active? I chose yes, and asked whether it could change later; the check lives in one query.
  • Should recomputed later pencairan be marked as edited? I chose no.

The SonarQube check on #27 failed, and the mobile dashboard showed "The main branch has no lines of code". Rather than re-running until it passed, I read the logs:

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

Standard principles applied and shown in this week's code: SOLID (single responsibility, open/closed, interface segregation, dependency inversion; see SOLID in this week's code), a deep module with a small interface, validation before any write, DRY shared rules, and an explicit fix for an N+1 query.

docs.title: The problem the design had to solve
docs.text:
Editing an old pencairan's nominal or tanggal changes the saldo at every later point, so every later pencairan's saldo_sebelum/saldo_sesudah receipt goes stale. The PO decided those must be recomputed. Two constraints shaped the solution:

  • Saldo cannot be replayed from zero. PILAH 1.0 opening balances were imported into Saldo with no transaksi behind them, so a sum of the ledger does not equal the stored saldo.
  • "Enough saldo" must hold at every later point, not only today. An edit that today's saldo covers can still overdraw a pencairan that happened between the edited one and now.

docs.title: Deep module: one entry point, the replay hidden behind it — 0856114
docs.text:
The view calls one method, PencairanService.edit_pencairan(user, pencairan, payload). The replay lives in a private helper:

api/services.py — PencairanService._hitung_ulang_saldo (excerpt)
        # PILAH 1.0 opening balances have no transaksi behind them, so the replay starts
        # from a stored snapshot: the first pencairan at or after `mulai`, minus the
        # setoran ordered before it (a setoran at the same instant comes first).
        pertama = min([pencairan, *lainnya], key=lambda cair: (cair.tanggal, str(cair.pk)))
        awal = pertama.saldo_sebelum - sum(
            (nilai for _, waktu, nilai in setoran if waktu <= pertama.tanggal), Decimal(0)
        )
        ...
        akhir_lama, _ = putar(pencairan.nominal, pencairan.tanggal)
        akhir_baru, snapshot = putar(nominal, tanggal)
        ...
        saldo.total_saldo += akhir_baru - akhir_lama

Three decisions are in these lines:

  1. Anchor on a stored snapshot, not on zero. The replay starts at the earliest moment the edit affects (mulai, the earlier of the old and new tanggal), from a saldo_sebelum that was exact when recorded.
  2. Replay twice, apply the difference. putar runs once with the old values and once with the new ones. Saldo moves by akhir_baru - akhir_lama instead of being overwritten, so any offset the replay cannot explain (for example a legacy balance) is kept rather than silently destroyed.
  3. One ordering rule. Events sort by (tanggal, setoran before pencairan, id), the same rule the saldo history and the Excel export already use, so the recomputed receipts agree with the history screen. Each pencairan re-applies the same round-down to whole rupiah as recording does.

The overdraw rule falls out of the replay: nilai > saldo_berjalan is checked at every pencairan, so a later one that would be paid from too little saldo rejects the edit. The coverage test 120c28b builds exactly that case: Rp 115.600 today would cover +Rp 20.000, but the next pencairan would then be paid Rp 250.000 from Rp 245.600.

docs.title: Validate first, then write — 8feca13
docs.text: The first version stored the revision and then validated the tanggal. It was correct (the transaction rolls back), but the order read wrong and made "nothing changed" impossible to reject cleanly. The service now works out the new values, rejects an empty change and an out-of-range tanggal, and only then writes the revision and the recompute, all in one transaction.atomic with the rows locked.

docs.title: DRY: one rule set for recording and editing — f9b70d8, f6a2ed7
docs.text: The nominal rules (positive, whole rupiah) and the tanggal rule (not in the future) were methods on the create serializer. The edit serializer needed the same, so both became module functions that both serializers call, instead of copies that could drift. The 7-day limit is one constant, BATAS_MUNDUR_TANGGAL_PENCAIRAN_HARI, which the service, the error message and the tests all read, and the app gets the resulting date from the API (tanggal_edit_minimum) rather than hard-coding 7.

docs.title: N+1 found and fixed — 0ea7252 → 7bceb58
docs.text: diperbarui and tanggal_edit_minimum each ran a query per row, so a page of 100 pencairan meant 200 extra queries. The list queryset now annotates both with Exists and a Subquery, and the serializer falls back to a query only for an instance that did not come from that queryset (the one an edit returns). A test pins the query count so it cannot silently grow back.

docs.title: Named permission class instead of operator composition — 3c4aac0
docs.text: Letting nasabah read their own pencairan needed "active pengurus or nasabah" on two actions. DRF's IsActivePengelola | IsNasabah works at runtime, but under mypy --strict its result is a private protocol type that get_permissions cannot be annotated with. A small named class, IsActivePengelolaOrNasabah, keeps the types honest, reads better at the call site, and is reused by PIL-230.

docs.title: Fixing the root cause, not the symptom — fd91ee8
docs.text: Saldo history disagreed with the stored saldo after a pencairan dropped sen. Patching the displayed number would have hidden it. The cause was that history debited only nominal, while the saldo actually lost nominal plus the dropped sen. Both history paths now debit saldo_sebelum - saldo_sesudah, the amount that really left, which needed no new column.

docs.title: Single Responsibility: one permission class per access rule — 3c4aac0
docs.text:
Each permission class answers one question, and the view only picks which one applies to an action. The combined rule reuses the two existing classes instead of repeating their checks.

class IsNasabah(BasePermission):
    message = "Endpoint ini hanya untuk nasabah"

    def has_permission(self, request: Request, view: APIView) -> bool:
        return request.user.is_authenticated and request.user.role == User.Role.NASABAH


class IsActivePengelolaOrNasabah(BasePermission):
    message = "Endpoint ini hanya untuk pengelola aktif atau nasabah"

    def has_permission(self, request: Request, view: APIView) -> bool:
        return IsActivePengelola().has_permission(request, view) or IsNasabah().has_permission(
            request, view
        )

    def get_permissions(self) -> list[BasePermission]:
        # Recording stays pengurus-only; nasabah may read their own riwayat.
        if self.action in ("list", "retrieve"):
            return [IsActivePengelolaOrNasabah()]
        return [IsActivePengelola()]

docs.title: Open/Closed: edit history as a new table, Pencairan unchanged — f0afdef
docs.text:
PIL-230 needed an audit trail for edits. Instead of adding version columns to Pencairan, which every existing reader (list, detail, saldo history, admin) would then have to account for, the history lives in a new append-only model. Existing code keeps working unmodified; only the new riwayat endpoint reads it.

class PencairanRevisi(models.Model):
    """A replaced version of a pencairan (PIL-230). Append-only: never edited or deleted."""

    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
    pencairan = models.ForeignKey(Pencairan, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="revisi")
    versi = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    ...
    # Why this version was replaced, by whom and when.
    alasan = models.CharField(max_length=255)
    diubah_oleh = models.ForeignKey(
        User, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="pencairan_revisi_dibuat"
    )
    diubah_pada = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    class Meta:
        db_table = "pencairan_revisi"
        ordering = ["pencairan", "versi"]
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["pencairan", "versi"], name="pencairan_revisi_unik"),
        ]

docs.title: Interface Segregation: an edit contract separate from the create contract — f0afdef, f9b70d8
docs.text:
An edit client should not have to send (or be able to change) the nasabah or bank sampah. PencairanEditSerializer exposes only the editable fields, all optional, plus the required alasan, while the validation rules are shared with the create serializer rather than copied.

class PencairanEditSerializer(serializers.Serializer[Any]):
    nominal = serializers.DecimalField(max_digits=14, decimal_places=2, required=False)
    metode = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=Pencairan.Metode.choices, required=False)
    tanggal = serializers.DateTimeField(required=False)
    keterangan = serializers.CharField(
        required=False, allow_blank=True, allow_null=True, max_length=255
    )
    alasan = serializers.CharField(required=True, max_length=255, ...)

    def validate_nominal(self, value: Decimal) -> Decimal:
        return _validate_nominal_pencairan(value)

    def validate_tanggal(self, value: datetime) -> datetime:
        return _validate_tanggal_pencairan(value)

docs.title: Dependency Inversion: the cubit depends on an abstraction — 1c2b0f2, 76aa268
docs.text:
On mobile, EditPencairanCubit depends on the abstract PencairanUseCases, not on the repository or HTTP client. The concrete implementation is supplied by dependency injection (injectable), so the test replaces it with a mocktail mock.

abstract class PencairanUseCases {
  ...
  Future<Either<NetworkException, Pencairan>> editPencairan(
    EditPencairanRequest request,
  );
}

@Injectable()
class EditPencairanCubit extends Cubit<EditPencairanState> {
  final PencairanUseCases _useCases;

  EditPencairanCubit(this._useCases) : super(const EditPencairanState());

class _MockUseCases extends Mock implements PencairanUseCases {}
...
      when(() => useCases.editPencairan(_request))

Liskov Substitution is the same boundary seen from the test side: any PencairanUseCases implementation, real or mocked, can be passed to the cubit without it behaving differently.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Competency level: 1

Code prevents OWASP A01 (Broken Access Control), the risk is named in the commit messages of the tests that guard it (on PIL-222 and PIL-230), and new endpoints were checked against it before merge.

docs.title: A01 · Broken Access Control, named in the commit
docs.text:
8ee88c1 test(pencairan): cover bank scoping of filtered riwayat (OWASP A01), in pilah-be #32.

Adding periode, nasabah_id and search to the pencairan list is exactly where a scoping bug appears: a user-supplied filter that widens the queryset would leak another bank's payouts.

The defence is ordering. The bank filter is the root of the queryset, and every user-supplied filter is chained onto it, so each one can only narrow the result further:

api/views.py
    def get_queryset(self) -> QuerySet[Pencairan]:
        qs = Pencairan.objects.filter(bank_sampah=_bank_sampah(self.request)).select_related(
            "nasabah", "bank_sampah", "dicatat_oleh"
        )
        nasabah_id = self.request.query_params.get("nasabah_id")
        search = self.request.query_params.get("search", "")
        if nasabah_id:
            qs = qs.filter(nasabah_id=nasabah_id)
        if len(search) >= 2:
            qs = qs.filter(nasabah__nama__icontains=search)
        return qs

nasabah_id is the dangerous one: it is a raw UUID from the client, and had it been applied to Pencairan.objects instead of to the scoped queryset, any pengurus could have read another bank's payouts by guessing an id.

The test creates a second bank with its own nasabah and pencairan, then asserts the caller sees only their own record under every filter shape — no filter, a search matching the other bank's nasabah name, and a periode:

api/tests.py — test_riwayat_never_shows_another_bank
        own = self._pencairan(self.siti, timezone.now())

        for query in ("", "?search=siti", "?periode=hari_ini"):
            with self.subTest(query=query):
                self.assertEqual(self._ids(query), {str(own.id)})

The other bank's nasabah is deliberately named "Siti Lain" so that ?search=siti matches it: if the scoping were wrong, this test fails rather than passing by luck.

Control Test Bank scoping applied before every user filter test_riwayat_never_shows_another_bank A nasabah_id from another bank returns an empty list, not that bank's rows same A search matching another bank's nasabah name returns nothing same

The reviewer confirmed this independently: "the queryset is always rooted at filter(bank_sampah=_bank_sampah(request)) before any filter is applied, so a nasabah_id or search matching another bank's data cannot leak".

docs.title: Why it matters here
docs.text: This is the SDS rule BR-01/BR-02 in practice: one database serves every bank sampah, so a query that forgets its organisation filter returns other organisations' data without raising an error. A test is the only thing that notices.

docs.title: A01 again on PIL-230 — 60e7256
docs.text:
test(pencairan): cover bank scoping and pengurus-only edit and riwayat (OWASP A01), in pilah-be #52.

The edit endpoint changes money and the revision history exposes who changed what, so both need two layers: the right role and the right organisation.

Caller PATCH /pencairan/:id GET /pencairan/:id/riwayat Pengurus of another bank 404 (the pencairan is outside their scoped queryset) 404 Nasabah who owns the pencairan 403 (pengurus only) 403 (pengurus only, per the PO)

After both attempts the test asserts the nominal and the saldo are unchanged, so a leak that "only" returned a 200 without saving would still fail.

docs.title: Related controls from the 26 Sep review fixes
docs.text:
These guard real weaknesses, but they are not yet named against an OWASP category in a commit, so they are listed here and not counted toward level 2:

Weakness Control Commit Admin writes bypassing the service could desynchronise a money ledger Pencairan and revisions are read-only in Django admin 9f4a428, 2af8c69 A backdated payout funded by a later deposit (business-logic flaw) Reject a tanggal before the nasabah's last activity 290bb1d Nasabah reading beyond their own records Nasabah queryset rooted at nasabah__user = request.user 3c4aac0 Money records changed without a trace Every edit stores the replaced version, editor, time and a required reason (append-only) c2ef8a4

The mobile tests isolate each layer from the one below it, so a failure points at one unit. 49 uses of mocks, stubs and Completers across 8 pencairan test files this week:

  • Reviews: Pascal's pilah-be #84 (PIL-300) reviewed. Gabriel's review of #89 answered.

Week 2 is claimed separately: IR Part B Sprint 1 Week 2.

docs.title: AI Literacy
docs.text:
Competency level: 3

AI used critically: its claims were checked against git history, the database and the tests before being acted on. Its plans were corrected where they clashed with how the team actually works. Every outward action (pushes, PR reviews, comments) waited for my decision. The prompt history is published below with personal data removed.

Two records of the same Claude Code session:

  • AI prompt history, 7–9 Oct: 23 prompts, built from the session transcript. Each tool call is one line, and personal data is removed.
  • Session export: Claude Code's own /export of the whole session, from the 2 Oct check on #64 to 9 Oct, with tool output collapsed as the export shows it. Local home-folder paths are shortened to ~; nothing else is changed.

docs.title: How AI was used this week
docs.text:
• Tool: Claude Code as an agent in VS Code across pilah-be, pilah-mobile and pilah-docs, Linear through Composio, GitHub through gh, and, new this week, the SonarQube CLI (sonar list issues), which reads SonarCloud results directly instead of through the website.
  • Guardrails: the workspace skills (tdd, ship), CI's own commands run locally, and the rules it keeps in memory from earlier weeks: phase-tagged commits, OWASP categories named in commits, replying inside review threads, never merging, and 3P in Bahasa.
  • My role: choosing the issue, deciding the design questions it raised (drop the column; start at 00:00 rather than 23:59), approving each outward action, and correcting it when it worked from the wrong assumption.

docs.title: Where verification changed the outcome
docs.text: Situation What happened It recommended PIL-341 (pencairan on web) as my second Sprint 2 issue The issue had to wait on teammates' web setup. I unassigned myself and told it why: in practice the team grabs issues first come, first served, so blocked issues just sit idle. It saved the rule "recommend only issues startable now", and its next suggestions followed it. My message said new prices could "start at every 23:59" It asked instead of guessing: 23:59 on the date shifts the price by a day. The answer (00:00 local) went into the date picker and the backend's offset rule. Its own plan said PUT with a price would return 422 While implementing, it noticed staging deploys the backend before testers get the new app, so a 422 would break editing for them. It changed course and said so in the summary instead of silently deviating. The tie-break test passed without any code It didn't fake a red: it explained that SQLite returns equal rows newest first, and Postgres doesn't. The fix went in as a [REFACTOR] with that reason in the commit. Validating on Postgres, which CI uses, with no Docker on the machine It ran Postgres 16 from a pip package. The bundled build lacked timezone data (invalid value for parameter "TimeZone": "UTC"); the cause was diagnosed and fixed by copying tzdata in. All 464 tests and the migration ran on the same database engine as CI. The migration had to be safe on real data It restored the team's production dump into a scratch database, migrated forwards, backwards and forwards again, and compared row counts. Then it dropped that database, because the dump holds personal data. A widget test showed the new list line overflowing at phone width The 112 px overflow was fixed. The same check on the edit sheet showed overflows in code that predates PIL-304, partly caused by the test font's wide glyphs, so it reported them instead of "fixing" shared widgets inside an unrelated PR. CI failed on pull_request but passed on push, twice It worked out the difference: pull_request merges the latest staging. Teammates' new tests used the dropped column (backend) or the old cubit constructor (mobile). Both were fixed on the branch, not by weakening the tests. A SonarCloud "composite assertion" finding Checked first: valid, because a failure wouldn't say which value was None. Split into two asserts, keeping plain assert because mypy narrows types only on that. Mobile diff coverage came out at 92% It flagged that 92% wouldn't support a 100% claim and added the missing tests, instead of writing "100%" on this page. A widget test couldn't see the success toast It found the toast was raised from a context the test's router had already removed. Rather than change app code for a test-harness detail, it moved the message choice into a pure, unit-tested function. That also fixed the Sonar issue. Gabriel's review on #89 said the test missed a case "only if setoran can carry sen" It checked that legacy setoran do carry sen before adding the test, then proved the test guards the loop by moving the rounding and watching it fail. Counting this week's IR evidence It first counted week 3 as 30 Sep – 6 Oct. When I showed it the course calendar, it recomputed (29 Sep – 5 Oct) and pointed out the risk of claiming the same 29 Sep merges in both week 2 and week 3.

docs.title: Example: "turns out we can just report this week's progress"
docs.text:
When I asked how to claim week 3, the AI first reported, accurately, that the week had almost no recorded development and suggested an honest "no activity" note. When I said this week's progress could be reported instead, it didn't just write pages from what existed:

It checked each competency against the rubric and stopped to ask where the evidence was short:

  • Team Development Management had no review of a teammate's MR.
  • Security named four OWASP categories, where level 2 needs five.

Both gaps were closed with real work, not wording: a review of Pascal's #84 that I approved before it was posted, and an allow-list for the jenis filters (A03), written test-first.

docs.title: Example: the design decisions stayed mine
docs.text:
PIL-304 had two choices that would be hard to undo: dropping a column that real data lives in, and how precisely a scheduled price can start. The AI didn't decide either on its own. It laid out a recommendation and the alternative, then waited:

When I asked what "picking a time of day" meant, it answered with a concrete case (13:00 on 15 Oct instead of 00:00) and the consequence of my choice (every scheduled price starts at local midnight; "Sekarang" covers immediate changes) before writing any code. My later "start at every 23:59" message got the same treatment: a question about which day was meant, not a guess.
